entry.title: Application by Raquel Gray [2026] FWC 4143
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission determined an unfair termination remedy application by a regulated road transport contractor, Ms Gray, against BESB Couriers after she was replaced on the Toukley delivery run upon returning from leave. The Commission found there was no valid reason for termination and that the Road Transport Industry Termination Code processes were not followed, so the termination was unfair. It ordered that a new services contract be entered into between BESB Couriers and Ms Gray personally.

Key holding: A regulated road transport contractor’s termination is unfair where there is no valid reason for termination and the processes under the Road Transport Industry Termination Code are not followed.

In summary, there was no valid reason for the termination of the services contract, and the processes in the Road Transport Code were not followed, in part because of a breakdown in communication and in part because BESB Couriers is a small business with l imited access to resources or relevant legal or human resources expertise. I am satisfied that the termination of the services contract was unfair.

entry.title: Mr Josateki Vunimasi & Mr Aminio Cava and Others v Woodward Foods Australia Pty Ltd & Mr Richard Tomasevic [2026] FWCFB 284
entry.content:
This was a Full Bench appeal concerning seven PALM scheme workers whose s 365 general protections dismissal applications named Woodward Foods as respondent, although their actual employer/dismisser was Whales. The Deputy President found no valid s 365 application because they did not allege dismissal in contravention of Part 3-1, and the Full Bench refused permission to appeal. The appeal also sought to raise joint employment and host-employer oral promise arguments not argued at first instance.

Key holding: For a valid s 365 application, the person must have been dismissed and must allege that the dismissal contravened Part 3-1; otherwise the Commission’s s 368 powers are not enlivened.

It is abundantly clear that the Deputy President applied the principle outlined in Milford. He properly determined that the Appellants were not entitled to make applications under s 365 and nor were the functions of the Commission under s 368 enlivened because the second criterion was not met.

entry.title: Application by Zion Alexander Guy [2026] FWC 3942
entry.content:
Zion Guy applied to the Fair Work Commission for an unfair deactivation remedy under s 536LU of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) after Uber deactivated him from its driver platform following rider complaints of apparent impairment and erratic driving. Uber contended the deactivation complied with the Fair Work (Digital Labour Platform Deactivation Code) Instrument 2024. The Commission dismissed the application, finding the deactivation consistent with the Code.

Key holding: The s 9 warning-bypass is available only where reasonable grounds exist and the operator commences the Division 3 process in a timely manner; long unexplained delay is inconsistent with that purpose.

However, I consider the exception in s 9 is available only if the process under Division 3 of the Code is commenced in a timely manner. Allowing it to be commenced after a long, unexplained delay would be inconsistent with the provision's apparent purpose of allowing the operator to bypass the warning obligation and move straight to deactivation.

entry.title: Kay and Commissioner of Taxation (Taxation and business) [2026] ARTA 2310
entry.content:
Matthew Kay objected to superannuation guarantee charge assessments for failing to make superannuation contributions for Daryl Marschke for 1 July 2019 to 30 June 2023. The Commissioner initially found Mr Marschke was not an employee but later reversed that position on delegation issues and assessed SGC. The Tribunal affirmed the objection decision.

Key holding: A contract is not wholly or principally for a person’s labour if it leaves the contractor free to do the work personally or employ others, even if the contractor in fact performs most of the work.

Even where a person has performed the bulk of the work under the contract, or it was the expectation of the parties that the person would do so, a contract that 'leaves the contractor free to do the work himself or employ other persons to carry it out' is not wholly or principally for the labour of the person.

entry.title: Australian Workers' Union v Chevron Australia Pty Ltd [2026] FCA 1492
entry.content:
The Australian Workers' Union alleged that Chevron breached s 323 of the Fair Work Act by deducting field loading and transport allowances from employees' pay during protected industrial action. The Federal Court held that the field loading allowance was captured by s 470(1) (the industrial action payment prohibition) and thus not payable, but the transport allowance was not captured because it did not relate to work performed during the industrial action.

Federal Court of Australia, 13 Oct 2026, [2026] FCA 1492

entry.title: Mr Liam Bruce Wright v Vrahos Contractors [2026] FWC 3917
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission dismissed an unfair dismissal application on its own initiative for want of prosecution after the applicant failed to attend a staff conciliation and then failed to respond to repeated Chambers correspondence and warnings. The decision turns on the applicant’s non-participation, not the merits of the unfair dismissal claim.

Key holding: Where an applicant’s conduct or omissions show they are no longer willing to participate in their own case, the Commission is not required to persevere with the application and may dismiss it for want of prosecution if procedural fairness has been afforded.

If an applicant's conduct or omissions show that they are no longer willing to participate in their own case , the Commission is not required to persevere with the application ( see Viavattene v Health Care Australia [[2013] FWCFB 2532] at [39]).

entry.title: Application by Raham Shahzad [2026] FWC 3914
entry.content:
Mr Shahzad applied for an unfair deactivation remedy under s 536LU of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) after Amazon deactivated him from the Amazon Flex digital labour platform. Amazon objected that he was not protected from unfair deactivation because he had not performed work on the platform on a regular basis for at least six months. The Fair Work Commission dismissed the application.

Key holding: For s 536LD(c), the Commission’s inquiry is limited to whether the person actually performed work and whether that work was performed on a regular basis for at least six months before deactivation.

The relevant inquiry under s 536LD(c) of the Act is limited to, first, whether a person has been performing work and secondly, whether such work was performed on a regular basis for a period of at least 6 months.

entry.title: Jovanovski v Billbergia Pty Ltd [2010] NSWSC 211
entry.content:
The plaintiff, a subcontract truck driver, slipped on grease on his truck ladder and fell about 2 metres, suffering lumbar, cervical and psychological sequelae. The NSW Supreme Court found breach of duty but held causation was not established under s 5D of the Civil Liability Act 2002, and entered a verdict for the defendant. entry.title: Australian Rail, Tram and Bus Industry Union (139V) v Loram Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 3157
entry.content:
The RTBU notified a dispute under s.739 of the Fair Work Act concerning whether Loram Pty Ltd must pay the 30% night shift penalty for all rostered hours of a night shift when employees are directed to finish early. Commissioner Lee construed the enterprise agreement, finding 'time worked' and 'work' consistently refer to actual physical work, and that penalty rates compensate for the inconvenience of actually working unsociable hours. The Commission determined employees are entitled to the night shift penalty only for hours they actually work.
